ai.title: Corpus Luteum Physiology
ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The corpus luteum is a transient endocrine gland formed after ovulation that secretes progesterone and estrogen to support the luteal phase and early pregnancy. Its function, regulation, and failure have direct implications for fertility, menstrual disorders, and early pregnancy loss.

b: Forms from granulosa and theca cells after ovulation
Produces ~20 mg/day progesterone in the luteal phase, rising to ~250 mg/day at term if pregnancy continues
If pregnancy does not occur, it involutes into the corpus albicans within 2 weeks
sections.p: After the dominant follicle releases the oocyte, the ruptured follicle wall remodels into the corpus luteum, a highly vascularised luteinised tissue that secretes steroid hormones for about 10‑14 days.

b: LH surge triggers luteinisation and angiogenesis
Estrogen maintains endometrial proliferation and cervical mucus quality
sections.p: Granulosa cells convert androgens from theca interna into estradiol via aromatase; luteinised cells shift to progesterone synthesis using cholesterol as substrate, driven by LH receptors.

b: LH peak → luteinisation; LH decline → luteolysis
hCG (produced by syncytiotrophoblast) binds LH receptors, prolonging progesterone output
Negative feedback: progesterone suppresses GnRH/LH release
sections.p: LH from the anterior pituitary is the primary luteotropic hormone; in early pregnancy, hCG mimics LH to sustain the corpus luteum until placental takeover.

t.b: Is luteal phase adequate? Low LH suggests luteal insufficiency; normal/high LH supports functional CL
Assesses CL function; <10 ng/mL indicates luteal phase defect
Confirms CL support; rising hCG >5 IU/L by day 8 post‑conception predicts viable pregnancy

b: Luteal phase defect – inadequate progesterone, often idiopathic or due to chronic stress, malnutrition, or endocrine disorders
Corpus luteum cyst – functional cyst persisting >2 cycles, may rupture causing acute abdomen
Premature luteolysis – seen with severe infection (e.g., malaria, HIV) or use of GnRH antagonists
sections.p: Failure of the corpus luteum to produce sufficient progesterone leads to luteal phase defect, infertility, or early miscarriage; over‑production can cause ovarian cysts.

t.b: Detects cystic CL; a solid, vascular CL suggests normal function, a thin‑walled cyst >3 cm may need observation
Low level confirms luteal insufficiency; if unavailable, rely on endometrial thickness on ultrasound

b: Progesterone supplementation (e.g., micronised progesterone) for luteal phase support in assisted reproduction
Watchful waiting for small functional CL cysts; intervene if pain, haemodynamic instability, or size >5 cm
Consider malaria or HIV screening in women with unexplained luteal failure in endemic areas
sections.p: Understanding CL physiology guides management of infertility, recurrent miscarriage, and ovarian cysts, especially where hormonal assays are limited.

b: Mid‑luteal progesterone <10 ng/mL = luteal phase defect
Ruptured CL cyst → sudden lower‑abdomen pain, guarding, possible haemoperitoneum; treat with analgesia, observation, or surgery if unstable
hCG rise >53 % over 48 h indicates viable early pregnancy
sections.p: Examiners test integration of endocrine cycles, interpretation of hormone assays, and emergency management of ruptured CL cysts.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with hypotension after suspected CL cyst rupture
